country.comment: The study exclusively examines rural sanitation infrastructure, regulation, and public policy across Chile's 16 regions grouped into three macrozones (North, Center, South).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, Section 1; PDF p. 5, Section 3.1, Tables 3-4

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive diagnostic statistics only; no inferential statistical test, regression coefficient, confidence interval, or p-value is reported. Note also that despite 'Investment' in the title and abstract, monetary capital investment estimates are not reported beyond monthly user fees (US$3.41-US$7.76).
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive institutional-technical diagnosis — no inferential numeric effect estimate reported. Nationwide, out of 2,441 officially recognized Rural Sanitation Services (RSS) under Law No. 20.998 (serving 2,308,071 inhabitants with drinking water), only 316 localities (13%) have wastewater collection or treatment infrastructure, benefiting 620,617 people (27% of the rural population with drinking water access), across 326 systems (306 operational wastewater treatment plants and 20 networked systems discharging untreated sewage; relative coverage 53% overall: 47% Center, 50% North, 61% South). Only 27% of evaluated systems perform adequately, whereas 73% show structural or operational failures (or lack evaluation data) and ~30% are in a critical state requiring urgent intervention (51% in the South, 34% Center, 15% North). Under uniform discharge regulations (DS 90/2000 and DS 46/2002) and Law No. 20.998's cost-recovery tariff rule (monthly wastewater fees of US$3.41-US$7.76; 44% municipal management, 41% partially subsidized committees, 13% unknown management), 96.3% of rural WWTPs fail to regularly monitor treated effluent quality (69.5% do not monitor at all, 26.8% monitor once a year, and 3.7% quarterly or more), while uncoordinated multi-agency investments produced multiple disjointed plants in 15 localities and concentrated 34% of facilities in small systems (<300 connections) whereas large systems (>600 connections, 32% of facilities) serve 58% of the treated population.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at <=2 by non-experimental design ceiling. Rated 2 because the study directly documents how legal, regulatory, financial, and institutional mechanisms operate empirically using national administrative cadasters and field-verified technical survey records (e.g., 93.86% operator registration vs. lagging licensing under Law 20.998; 96.3% non-monitoring of effluent under uniform DS 90/DS 46 standards given cost-recovery monthly tariffs of US$3.41-US$7.76; 15 localities with duplicate plants from fragmented agency interventions; 20 networked systems discharging untreated sewage linked to procurement/contractual/administrative execution failures).
